routes.description: Establish that Jesus personally claimed divine identity by reading his titles, sayings, prerogatives, and reception cumulatively within a first-century Jewish two-powers framework and by defending that interpretation against delegated-authority alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant Jewish framework can include distinguishable divine figures, Jesus applies that identity framework to himself through words and functions, and the cumulative evidence is not adequately explained by mere agency, exalted humanity, or later attribution.

motionBridge.description: Connect Jesus's own claimed titles, authority, and functions to personal participation in divine identity rather than merely to later beliefs about him.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish scripture supplied a recognizable framework of distinguishable figures sharing Yahweh's identity and that Jesus located himself within it.
Show that Jesus's Son, Lord, Son of Man, divine-name, unity, and preexistence language communicates more than messianic or representative status.
Show that Jesus's claims to equal honor, universal judgment, life-giving authority, resurrection power, and premundane glory identify him with divine functions.
Connect followers' devotion and opponents' accusations to Jesus's self-claims while establishing that the resulting high christology is early rather than a late development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how receiving authority, serving, and distinguishing himself from the Father can coexist with prior divine identity through incarnation and exaltation.
Establish when worship language and hostile reactions reliably corroborate the intended force of Jesus's claims.

routes.description: Defeat the claim that Jesus personally identified himself as God by showing that the cited language, functions, and honors remain explicable through divine name-bearing, delegated agency, messianic or ideal-human status, and later high christology.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative cannot bridge from disputed texts and received authority to Jesus's own divine identity because viable agency readings remain, contrary dependence language persists, or early Christian portrayals do not establish Jesus's historical self-claim.

motionBridge.description: Show that exalted status, divine authorization, name-bearing, or later portrayal does not by itself establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish representatives could bear God's name, exercise transmitted authority, and receive deference without being identical with Yahweh.
Show that unity, glory, judgment, forgiveness, miraculous power, and other assertedly divine features are received by Jesus or extended to disciples.
Provide non-divine readings of the principal Johannine, Synoptic, Danielic, and Pauline terms and passages used to infer divine identity.
Separate claims made by Jesus from followers' devotion, authorial framing, later high christology, and historically disputed interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that blasphemy accusations, stoning attempts, and other reactions may reflect misunderstanding or charges that do not require a divine-identity claim.
Distinguish homage language applicable to non-divine recipients from cultic service that would uniquely identify its recipient as God.

sections.title: Two powers, divine name-bearing, and Jewish agency
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the controlling historical framework for deciding whether distinguishable Yahweh figures and divine name-bearing imply shared divine identity or delegated representation.

sections.title: Jesus's sayings, titles, and scriptural allusions
sections.rationale: The motion centrally depends on whether Son, Lord, Son of Man, unity, preexistence, and divine-name language constitutes Jesus's personal divine claim or permits non-divine readings.

sections.title: Divine prerogatives, dependence, and delegated authority
sections.rationale: Claims involving judgment, resurrection, life, forgiveness, glory, and Sabbath authority must be tested against language of receipt, dependence, prayer, and comparable grants to disciples.

sections.title: Worship, early devotion, and hostile reactions
sections.rationale: Followers' prayers and homage and opponents' blasphemy reactions may corroborate Jesus's intended claim, but their semantic force and reliability require independent assessment.

sections.title: Historical self-claim and christological development
sections.rationale: The debate requires separating Jesus's own claims from Gospel framing and early Christian christology while assessing Synoptic and Johannine differences, Pauline material, and proposed development.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Old Testament portrayals of two distinguishishable figures acting as Yahweh establish a two-powers framework within which Jesus identifies himself as one divine power.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening continues in Wood's voice and develops the two-powers thesis announced immediately beforehand.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative's controlling Jewish-scriptural framework and therefore requires no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly develops the framework assigned to this constructive move with several promised scriptural examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-powers thesis is recoverable, but 'divine figures' and the move from acting as Yahweh to sharing divine identity need sharper criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical framework claim outruns the excerpt's brief appeal to numerous passages and does not yet compare agency readings.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but the bridge from distinguishable Yahweh-associated figures to two divine powers and then Jesus remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It invokes a named scholarly formulation and scriptural examples, but the representative cases and rival agency warrant are underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable two-powers framework, though it does not by itself complete Jesus's identification within it.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt primarily constructs its own framework and does not substantially engage a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly asserts one God alongside numerous Old Testament passages containing two divine figures and announces examples.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus presents himself as the unique Son, David's heavenly Lord, and Daniel's cloud-riding Son of Man, thereby claiming the identity of a heavenly divine power.
moves.attributionBasis: This extended textual argument remains within Wood's uninterrupted affirmative opening and uses his announced category of what Jesus says.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly develops Jesus's titles and Danielic trial language without answering an earlier opposing locked move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely presents the Son of Man and right-hand-of-Power material assigned to its constructive proposition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed allusion and conclusion are clear, but 'divine power' is not sufficiently distinguished from an exalted heavenly agent.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Danielic identification is well specified, while the further divine-identity conclusion needs acknowledgment of exalted-agent readings.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Daniel 7 allusion supports heavenly status, but heavenly enthronement does not without another bridge establish participation in God's identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites the trial saying and Daniel 7 specifically, yet it compresses comparison with non-identity interpretations of the cloud rider.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sayings-and-titles bridge through one of the affirmative's principal claimed self-identifications.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span advances the affirmative reading without sufficiently developing a live alternative for a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt connects Jesus's trial language about the right hand of Power and clouds with Daniel 7's Son of Man.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Jesus claims divine status by assuming Yahweh's roles as universal judge and raiser of the dead while requiring honor equal to the Father's.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood remains the sole speaker and explicitly transitions from what Jesus says to what Jesus does in support of his affirmative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative's principal divine-functions case and has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly adduces judgment, resurrection, and equal-honor language corresponding to the assigned proposition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed functions and textual basis are clear; the exclusivity premise and significance of granted judgment remain implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Equal honor strongly supports the inference, but the passage's giving and sending language makes an unqualified identity conclusion somewhat stronger than shown.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The combination of universal judgment, resurrection, and equal honor yields a strong inference, with one bounded exclusivity bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: John 5 is quoted specifically and supports the functions asserted, though received-authority language and rival readings are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly and substantially supports the central exclusive-divine-functions bridge using several principal prerogatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed delegated-authority interpretation is considered in this constructive excerpt, so meaningful charity is not tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes John 5 on all judgment being given to the Son and equal honor, then adds resurrection authority.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: The earliest Christians treated Jesus as divine Lord and creative Word, applied Yahweh's name and honors to him, and directed worship, prayer, hymns, baptism, and liturgy toward him.
moves.attributionBasis: The material completes Wood's opening before the moderator explicitly announces the end of David Wood's statement and Alex's turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies follower-devotion evidence for early high christology and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly enumerates the worship, prayer, hymnic, baptismal, and liturgical practices assigned to the proposition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practices are clearly listed, but 'earliest Christians,' 'full array,' and the inference to divine identity need narrower sourcing.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cumulative devotional pattern is probative, but its date, uniformity, and bearing on Jesus's own claim require explicit qualification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The practices support early exalted devotion, but the bridge from followers' conduct to Jesus's personal historical self-claim remains material.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports cumulative corroboration, while its indirect relation to Jesus's own self-claim limits completion of that bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move lists positive devotional evidence without presenting a developed alternative explanation of those practices.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists worship, prayer, hymns, baptism, liturgy, and doxology directed toward Jesus as a cumulative pattern.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus's appeal to Psalm 82 answers the charge of claiming deity by comparing his title with non-Yahweh beings called gods and by identifying himself as God's consecrated and sent Son.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator transfers the podium to Alex, whose opening then explicitly addresses David's two-powers interpretation and develops this counterreading.

components.text: Whether Jesus's Son language necessarily communicates divine identity rather than representative or non-Yahweh status.

response.rationale: The reply expressly argues that Psalm 82 supplies non-Yahweh beings called gods and states that Jesus's consecrated-and-sent Son language defeats the identity inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive inference from Jesus's title to divine identity and supplies a textual defeating alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed Psalm 82 inference, its comparison class, and the consecrated-and-sent qualification are all plainly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a targeted alternative reading rather than claiming that the passage conclusively disproves every divine reading.

charity.alternative: Jesus invokes Psalm 82 while still distinguishing himself as the uniquely consecrated Son.
charity.decisiveQualification: The passage may rebut an immediate blasphemy charge without exhaustively defining Jesus's identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If non-Yahweh beings can receive god language, the title alone does not entail identity; the inference is explicit and consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply closely uses Psalm 82 and Jesus's sent-Son wording, with a bounded gap regarding the wider Johannine context.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports textual underdetermination for a principal Johannine saying and attacks a central affirmative inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes Jesus's distinctive sent status, though it underdevelops how that distinction might strengthen rather than weaken the affirmative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts beings called gods but not Yahweh with Jesus's defense that he is the Father's set-apart and sent Son.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even if Jesus's 'I am' language evokes Exodus, Jewish traditions permit a non-Yahweh representative to bear God's name and exercise God's authority, so name-bearing does not establish identity with Yahweh.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor remains the uninterrupted speaker, introduces John 8 as another major christological claim, and carries the argument through the final delivered context row.

components.text: Whether Yahweh-associated name and authority language entails shared divine identity rather than authorized representation.

response.rationale: The reply identifies a Jewish name-bearing representative tradition and states the defeating consequence that Exodus resonance does not establish identity with Yahweh.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the identity inference underlying the affirmative framework and supplies a historically framed agency alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The agency alternative is clear, although the extent and representativeness of the referenced Jewish tradition remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording appropriately presents a contextual possibility and concedes the potential Exodus imagery rather than claiming decisive disproof.

charity.alternative: Jesus's 'I am' language intentionally evokes Exodus and therefore signals Yahweh's identity.
charity.decisiveQualification: An intentional divine-name echo can still function through a non-Yahweh authorized bearer in the cited tradition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A relevant Jewish tradition is identified, but representative texts and their proximity to the Gospel usage are not documented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central name-bearing-agency bridge and attacks the affirmative framework's identity criterion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the affirmative's strongest lexical premise and targets the disputed identity consequence rather than denying the echo.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes Exodus 3 imagery but appeals to early Jewish texts endowing non-Yahweh representatives with Yahweh's name and authority.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: John 8:58 can present Jesus as the fulfillment eternally planned in Abraham's promised redemption rather than asserting Jesus's personal preexistence or identity with Yahweh.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation remains within O'Connor’s opening statement and develops his previously established critical interpretation.

components.text: Whether Jesus's preexistence and divine-name language requires personal preexistence and divine identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive textual component but offers only a tentative alternative and partly concedes the affirmative reading.

precisionFindings.rationale: The promised-fulfillment proposal and its acknowledged difficulty with the present tense are both recoverable and carefully bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly labels the reading possible and a suggestion, then expressly acknowledges contrary linguistic pressure.

charity.alternative: The present-tense 'I am' asserts Jesus's personal preexistence before Abraham.
charity.decisiveQualification: The alternative proposed is possible but remains linguistically strained by the present tense.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Abrahamic-promise context gives some support, while the crucial grammar and common-tradition premise remain only suggested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports textual underdetermination of a principal Johannine saying, albeit with acknowledged weakness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states the strongest affirmative difficulty against its own proposal and does not overstate the alternative's success.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: An attempt to stone Jesus does not establish that his opponents correctly understood him as claiming deity, because Johannine opponents repeatedly misunderstand him and blasphemy accusations can arise from broader alleged offenses.
moves.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted opening statement explicitly examines the significance of blasphemy accusations and compares Jesus with Stephen.

components.text: Whether hostile reactions reliably corroborate that Jesus intended a divine-identity claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive reliability premise behind using stoning or blasphemy reactions as corroboration.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability objection is clear, though the broad characterization that opponents consistently misunderstand risks overgeneralizing distinct episodes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The recurrent-misunderstanding motif substantially weakens reaction evidence, but does not show that every hostile interpretation is incorrect.

charity.alternative: The stoning attempt reflects an accurate recognition that Jesus made a blasphemous divine claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Narrative opponents' recurrent misunderstanding prevents their reaction from serving as independent proof without contextual confirmation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic point is valid: a reaction by frequently mistaken interpreters cannot independently establish the correctness of their interpretation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Johannine misunderstanding motif is a specific relevant feature, though broader blasphemy contexts are only asserted here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary reaction-and-obscurity bridge and directly limits hostile reaction evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the evidential use of the reaction rather than denying that the opponents may have perceived some exalted claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly invokes the Gospel theme that Jesus's opponents repeatedly misunderstand him when explaining the stoning reaction.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Scriptural interaction between Yahweh and the angel of Yahweh supports two distinguishable heavenly powers rather than reducing the angel to a merely delegated human representative.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Wood’s rebuttal, after which Wood explicitly summarizes his opening and answers O'Connor’s delegated-authority proposal.

components.text: Whether the Yahweh-associated angel is adequately explained as a merely authorized representative rather than a distinguishable divine figure.

response.rationale: The Genesis 22 interaction contacts the agency alternative by emphasizing shifts between God and the angel, but the excerpt does not fully exclude representation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It addresses the decisive agency issue with a concrete passage but leaves the representative explanation materially available.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended distinction argument is discernible, but the excerpt's interrupted quotation does not fully articulate its identity criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The textual alternation supports distinction and association, but the stronger two-divine-powers conclusion needs comparison with agency conventions.

charity.alternative: The angel speaks for Yahweh under ordinary authorized-agency conventions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The textual interaction and shifting identification require explanation but do not by themselves eliminate representative speech.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The interaction supports distinction, but association plus distinction does not without a further premise establish two divine powers.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genesis 22 is a concrete relevant case, although the selected evidence is incomplete and does not compare agency interpretation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central name-bearing-agency bridge, but only through one incompletely developed example.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move reaches the agency alternative through the passage, yet does not fully address the alternative's established mechanism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt begins a close comparison of God and the angel of Yahweh in Genesis 22, highlighting their distinction and interaction.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Stephen's vision and prayer to Jesus, together with the earliest Christians calling on Jesus's name, show Jesus receiving Yahweh-associated devotion within roughly two years of the crucifixion.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood explicitly turns to O'Connor’s Stephen example and sustains the rebuttal through Stephen’s prayer and the earliest Christian invocation of Jesus.

components.text: Whether hostile reactions accurately disclose the intended force of Jesus's own words.

response.rationale: Early invocation of Jesus is relevant contrary material about devotion, but it does not answer whether hostile interpreters reliably understood Jesus's claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move supplies issue-bearing devotion evidence while leaving the target's decisive hostile-reaction reliability demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The invocation and dating claim are clear, though 'earliest Christians' and equivalence with calling on Yahweh require bounded qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence supports very early devotion, but exact dating and equivalence between invocations are stated more strongly than defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Early invocation supports early high devotion, but followers' practice still requires a bridge to Jesus's personal self-claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's conversion chronology and invocation language are concrete, with compressed dating and semantic-equivalence warrants.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the self-claim distinction by supplying early corroboration, though it remains indirect evidence of Jesus's own claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops positive early-devotion evidence without directly considering a live alternative interpretation of that devotion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Christians calling on Jesus's name with Yahweh invocation and dates the practice by Paul's conversion roughly two years after crucifixion.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus receives and then delegates glory, judgment, and forgiveness, showing that possession of these allegedly divine prerogatives can reflect transmitted authority rather than personal identity as God.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor continues his rebuttal, explicitly answers Wood’s John 17 argument, and extends the same delegation principle to judgment and forgiveness.

components.text: Whether judgment and forgiveness uniquely identify their possessor as God.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies delegation to disciples as defeating the exclusivity premise behind the affirmative's prerogative inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the decisive exclusivity warrant and states the consequence that possession need not establish deity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The transferable-prerogative objection and its examples of judgment and forgiveness are clearly and consistently formulated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is appropriately limited to defeating necessity: delegated prerogatives do not by themselves prove personal divine identity.

charity.alternative: Jesus exercises divine prerogatives in a unique and categorically superior manner.
charity.decisiveQualification: Some cited prerogatives are nevertheless explicitly extended to disciples, defeating a simple exclusivity inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexamples validly defeat the inference that any possession of these functions necessarily entails deity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply supplies specific judgment and forgiveness grants, with a bounded gap concerning qualitative differences from Jesus's authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central shared-prerogatives bridge against one of the affirmative's principal arguments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly attacks the unqualified exclusivity premise, though it gives limited treatment to differences in scope and source.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites judgment over Israel promised to disciples and authority concerning forgiveness as counterexamples to exclusive divine possession.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The Gospels' pervasive misunderstanding and the Synoptic messianic-secret motif make it difficult to treat the record as evidence that Jesus clearly and publicly communicated a personal claim to be God.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person rebuttal follows Alex's identified speaking turn and directly addresses David's communication argument.

components.text: Whether Jesus clearly communicated the proposed divine identity through his sayings and titles.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly challenges the clarity premise, though obscurity alone does not decide what the disclosed sayings ultimately mean.

precisionFindings.rationale: The messianic-secret tension is clear, but 'every time' and the contrast with public divine-name claims are rhetorically broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The motif creates a real tension with obvious public disclosure, though secrecy about messiahship need not equal denial of every divine implication.

charity.alternative: Jesus genuinely claimed divine identity through indirect, progressively disclosed sayings.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect progressive disclosure can coexist with secrecy, so obscurity limits clarity evidence rather than disproving the claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The tension between pervasive secrecy and allegedly obvious proclamation is cogent, with a bounded gap concerning progressive disclosure.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Synoptic messianic-secret motif is a specific textual feature, but its application to divine identity is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reaction-and-obscurity bridge and bears materially on claimed clarity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the disclosure question but tends to frame the affirmative as claiming unambiguous, universally understood public speech.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an allegedly obvious public divine-name claim with the Synoptic pattern of concealed identity and recurrent misunderstanding.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Jesus's acceptance of proskynesis does not establish deity because the term can denote bodily homage to human authorities, whereas the New Testament uses distinct language for cultic service reserved for God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly pivots to worship terminology and sustains a lexical and comparative scriptural argument until the rebuttal closes.

components.text: Whether worship language directed toward Jesus is semantically unique to deity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive semantic-exclusivity premise and provides New Testament counterexamples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument properly defeats inference from proskynesis alone without claiming that every act directed to Jesus is merely civil homage.

charity.alternative: The context of proskynesis to Jesus makes it genuinely cultic despite the word's broader range.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The human-recipient counterexamples decisively show that the term alone is insufficient to establish deity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific New Testament examples support the semantic range, with only contextual comparison of Jesus passages left compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very strongly supports the subsidiary worship-semantics bridge and limits a significant corroborating argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately targets a lexical inference while leaving room for contextual evidence to distinguish particular instances.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Philippians 2 depicts a preexistent divine being who voluntarily assumes human likeness and receives universal homage, rather than an ordinary image-bearing human elevated only afterward.
moves.attributionBasis: David identifies Alex's use of a scholarly reading, quotes and interprets the hymn's sequence, and concludes with its application of Isaiah's Yahweh language.

components.text: Whether early high christology is better explained as later elevation rather than preexistent incarnation.
Whether servant status and received exaltation imply merely delegated non-divine status.

moves.proposition: Jesus's use of the Septuagint's doubled Kyrios formula points to Yahweh and, alongside the shared conclusions of followers and enemies, supports an intentionally veiled but genuine divine claim.

components.text: Whether indirect or veiled language can nevertheless communicate a genuine divine claim.
Whether Jesus's scriptural wording points specifically to Yahweh rather than generic lordship.

response.rationale: The Septuagintal doubled-Kyrios observation contacts the obscurity demand by proposing a specific veiled Yahweh allusion, though its exclusivity is not fully shown.

moves.proposition: Jesus's receipt of authority is compatible with prior divine identity because the divine Son assumes servant status in incarnation and is subsequently exalted, as reflected across Daniel 7, Philippians 2, John 1, and Matthew.
moves.attributionBasis: Wood links the objection about granted power to Daniel 7 and then develops a cross-text incarnation-and-exaltation account.

components.text: Whether receipt of authority is incompatible with prior divine identity.
Whether service and delegation establish that Jesus is only an authorized non-divine agent.

response.rationale: The reply justifies evaluating granted authority within an incarnation-and-exaltation sequence and answers that replacement demand by linking divine status, servant form, and subsequent grant.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly reconciles the target's dependence evidence through a stated incarnation model rather than merely asserting compatibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed sequence—prior divine status, servant incarnation, service, and exalted grant—is stable and expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move establishes a coherent compatibility explanation without claiming that grant language alone independently proves preexistent divinity.

charity.alternative: Receiving all authority indicates that Jesus previously lacked it and therefore was not intrinsically divine.
charity.decisiveQualification: Within an incarnation account, functional servant status and later exaltation can explain receipt without denying prior identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The incarnation model coherently reconciles divine status with servant dependence, conditional on independently supporting its preexistence premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Philippians 2 and Matthew's grant language concretely support the sequence, with cross-text synthesis carrying one bounded warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very strongly supports the subsidiary incarnation-reconciliation bridge and directly answers the received-authority objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accepts the force of received-authority language and supplies a substantive reconciliation rather than dismissing the objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt combines being in God's nature, taking servant form, living as servant, receiving worship, and being given universal authority.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The lack of early literary evidence for a two-powers controversy weakens the claim that a settled first-century two-powers framework governed how Jesus's hearers would interpret divine figures or his trial language.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor asks for historical support and reads McGrath's conclusion that the controversy leaves no clear trace even in second-century materials.

components.text: Whether a settled first-century two-powers interpretive framework is historically attested.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the affirmative's historical-attestation premise and cites scholarly evidence said not to support dating the controversy even to the second century.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks a decisive historical premise of the framework and states the consequence for audience interpretation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge carefully distinguishes possible origins from evidential support for dating the controversy and states the relevant historical scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited formulation denies evidential support while expressly allowing that the controversy could have arisen earlier.

charity.alternative: Scriptural patterns existed before later rabbinic labeling of a formal two-powers controversy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Earlier conceptual patterns remain possible, but they do not establish a settled first-century interpretive framework without attestation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The absence-of-attestation point does not disprove antecedents, but validly weakens claims of a settled, hearer-governing framework.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A directly relevant scholarly assessment is quoted, though the underlying surveyed corpus is not independently presented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central two-powers-framework bridge at its crucial historical-recognition premise.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the distinction between conceptual antecedents and a historically governing controversy, which is the decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes McGrath's conclusion that surveyed evidence does not support dating the controversy even to the second century, while allowing possibility.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.proposition: Different authorial emphases explain the Synoptics' omission of Johannine-style sayings, while Mark's progressive disclosure and Paul's early material show that divine christology was neither uniquely Johannine nor necessarily late.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is explicitly addressed to David Wood, and the extended answer follows his argumentative themes and first-person debate strategy.

components.text: Whether early sources independently support divine christology without relying on a late Johannine framework.
Whether Synoptic reticence is evidence against divine self-disclosure rather than differing progressive emphasis.

response.rationale: The reply appeals to distinct authorial emphases, Markan progression, Q, and Paul to answer lateness and obscurity, though the selected span develops these supports unevenly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive development demand but provides a compressed rather than fully demonstrated early-source comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The authorial-emphasis and early-source answer is discernible, but the excerpt is fragmented and its claims about opponents' source use are broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Different emphases and early material make development less necessary, but do not by themselves establish Jesus's historical self-understanding.

charity.alternative: Johannine divine sayings reflect a later christological development absent from the Synoptics.
charity.decisiveQualification: Different literary emphases and early Pauline material can weaken an argument from Synoptic omission, though they do not erase source differences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Authorial emphasis can explain omission, but possibility of differing emphasis is not by itself a probability argument against development.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Mark, Q, and Paul are specifically invoked, yet their relevant passages and the claimed progressive pattern are compressed in the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central self-claim distinction and development account through claimed early independent evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the lateness and omission case but partly substitutes criticism of source selectivity for a complete comparative explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts skepticism toward John with appeal to Q, Mark, and Paul, then proposes differing Synoptic authorial emphases.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Even granting that Paul held a high christology does not establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God, because Pauline interpretation remains distinct from the historical question of Jesus's own self-understanding.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the Philippians question to Alex first, and the response repeatedly states his own uncertainty and priorities.

components.text: Whether early Pauline high christology establishes Jesus's own historical self-claim.
Whether the interpretation of Philippians resolves the distinct historical question of Jesus's self-understanding.
Whether early follower devotion establishes what Jesus personally claimed.

response.rationale: The reply grants Pauline high christology for argument's sake and expressly states that it remains secondary to the distinct question of Jesus's own claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly isolates and defeats the inference from early follower or Pauline belief to Jesus's personal historical self-understanding.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between Pauline christology and Jesus's personal claim is sharply stated, with uncertainty about Pauline interpretation expressly bracketed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical non-entailment is categorical but properly limited: even granted high christology does not itself establish Jesus's self-claim.

charity.alternative: Very early Pauline high christology corroborates traditions rooted in Jesus's own claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early corroboration can raise plausibility but still requires an independent transmission bridge to Jesus's historical self-understanding.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is explicit and valid: a follower's early belief does not by itself entail the historical subject's own claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument primarily establishes a logical evidential boundary and appropriately grants rather than disputes the contested Pauline premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central self-claim-distinction bridge and reaches the motion's decisive historical attribution issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the strongest Pauline premise and identifies precisely what additional bridge would still be needed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grants Pauline high christology while distinguishing that question from whether Jesus personally claimed to be God.
